howItWorks.intro: A campground budget is really three different price tiers stacked together, not one number. Private RV parks and resorts with full hookups typically run $45–75 a night; public campgrounds — state parks, national parks, national forests, Corps of Engineers lakes — usually land in the $20–40 range with partial or no hookups; and free camping (BLM land, national forest dispersed sites, Harvest Hosts, a single night in a big-box lot) costs $0 but drops the hookups entirely. This calculator sorts your trip into those three buckets and multiplies each by a representative nightly rate so you get a total that reflects how you actually plan to camp, not a single flat average.

rules.name: Total Cost
rules.explanation: Average rates for private and public campgrounds.

howItWorks.outro: The $55 and $30 figures are national averages — a full-hookup site near a national park gate or on the coast in summer can run $80–120, while a no-frills gravel pad in rural farm country might be $25. The split between private, public, and free nights moves your total far more than the exact per-night figure does: shifting two or three nights from a private resort to a state park or a free BLM site can cut a two-week trip's campground bill by $150–300. Re-run the numbers once you have real reservations in hand, and swap in the actual quoted rates for anywhere you've already booked.

faq.question: How much do RV campgrounds cost per night?
faq.answer: Private RV parks and resorts with full hookups typically run $45–75 a night nationally, and can top $100 near national park entrances or on the coast in peak season. Public campgrounds — state parks, national forests, Corps of Engineers lakes — usually run $20–40 a night for a partial-hookup or no-hookup site. Free camping (BLM dispersed land, national forest dispersed sites, Harvest Hosts, some casino and big-box lots) costs $0 in fees but comes with no hookups.

faq.question: Is a Thousand Trails or Passport America membership worth it?
faq.answer: It depends on your nights, not just the discount percentage. Passport America (roughly $44/year) cuts private-park rates about in half but is usually capped to a night or two per stay at each park, so it helps most if you're moving frequently between different private parks. Thousand Trails charges a much larger annual zone fee (often $500–700 for one zone) but drops most in-system nights to $0 — it tends to pay off only for people logging 25+ nights a year at participating parks, which fits full-timers and snowbirds more than a two-week vacation.

faq.question: How do I budget for boondocking?
faq.answer: Boondocking removes the nightly camping fee, but not the cost — it shifts spending to generator fuel, extra battery or solar capacity, and the dump-and-fill stops you'll need every 4–7 days depending on tank size. Most boondocking RVers still budget one paid night (private park, $45–75) every few days specifically to dump tanks, fill fresh water, and run laundry.

faq.question: What's the cost difference between state park and national park camping?
faq.answer: State park campgrounds usually run $20–35 a night and often include electric hookups. National park campgrounds tend to run $20–30 a night but rarely offer hookups at all, so you're relying on tank capacity or a generator during allowed hours. Both typically require booking through Recreation.gov or the state's own reservation system 3–6 months ahead for summer dates, and both usually cap consecutive-night stays around 14 days.

faq.question: How accurate are the $55 and $30 default rates?
faq.answer: They're broad national averages, useful for a first-pass budget before you've booked anything. Real rates swing widely: a private park in a major metro area or near a national park gate can run $80–120, while a rural or off-season private park can be $35–45. Once you have a route, pull actual listed rates for 3–4 parks along it and adjust your private/public night split rather than trusting the defaults for a final number.

howWeCalculate.intro: Campground budgeting comes down to a weighted average across three cost tiers that can each swing by a factor of three depending on region, season, and hookup type — a flat per-night guess rarely holds up over a real trip.
steps: Split your total nights into the tiers you'll actually use: private RV parks and resorts, public campgrounds (state parks, national parks, national forests, Corps of Engineers lakes), and free sites (boondocking, Harvest Hosts, driveway or lot overnights).
The calculator multiplies private nights by the private-park average ($55) and public nights by the public-park average ($30), then adds the two — free nights contribute $0 by definition.
Total nights is a cross-check, not a separate cost input — it should equal private plus public plus free nights, so a mismatch flags a miscount before you book anything.
The result splits into a total dollar figure and an average per night, which is the number worth weighing against your fuel budget and daily food spend when you build a full trip budget.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These are planning-stage averages, not quotes. Peak-season coastal parks, holiday weekends, and anywhere near a national park entrance regularly run 40–80% above these baselines; off-season and inland public campgrounds often run below them. Pull three or four real listings from Recreation.gov, ReserveAmerica, or the park's own site before finalizing a budget.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this before you build a route, not after — knowing your likely campground spend changes how many nights you can afford to linger somewhere versus keep moving.
scenarios: Planning a multi-week trip and deciding how many nights you can afford at full-hookup private parks versus how many need to be public or free to stay on budget.
Comparing a Thousand Trails or Passport America membership's annual cost against how much it would actually save on your specific mix of nights.
Building a boondocking-heavy itinerary and figuring out how many paid nights you still need for laundry, a water fill-up, and a real shower.
Planning a snowbird or seasonal stay where state park camping caps out around 14–21 consecutive nights and you need a private park to bridge the gap.
Sanity-checking a trip after booking a few sites, to see if the remaining nights need to skew cheaper to hit a target total.

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Adds Up
sections.body: RV campground costs aren't a single rate — they're three different markets. Private RV parks and resorts (KOA, Sun RV, independent parks) charge for full hookups, wifi, a pool, and often a rec room, and that convenience runs $45–75 a night in most of the country, climbing past $100 near national park gates or on the coast in summer. Public campgrounds — state parks, national parks, national forest campgrounds, and Corps of Engineers lakes — trade some or all hookups for a lower rate, typically $20–40 a night, often in a nicer setting. Free camping — BLM dispersed sites, national forest dispersed sites, Harvest Hosts, or a single night in a big-box parking lot — costs nothing but comes with no hookups and sometimes no cell signal. Enter how many nights fall into each bucket and this calculator multiplies private nights by $55 and public nights by $30 (national averages), leaving free nights at $0, to give you a total and a per-night average.

sections.title: Where Membership Programs Fit In
sections.body: The three-tier split above is the baseline; membership programs change the math within it without changing which bucket a night belongs to. Passport America roughly halves the rate at participating private parks, so a $60 site can drop to $30 — but the discount is usually capped to one or two nights per stay at each park and often blacked out during peak season, so read the restrictions before counting on it. Thousand Trails works differently: you pay an annual zone fee (commonly $500–700 for a single zone, more for multi-zone access) and most nights inside the system then cost $0, which only beats paying per-night if you're realistically logging 25–30+ nights a year at member parks. Escapees, Good Sam, and KOA Rewards give smaller 10–15% discounts that add up over a long trip but won't move you into a cheaper tier by themselves. None of these show up as a separate field in the calculator — instead, lower your assumed private-park rate manually if a membership covers most of your private nights, since the $55 default is an unmembered average.

sections.title: A Worked Example: 14 Nights, Three Lodging Types
sections.body: Say you're routing a two-week trip through the Southwest: 4 nights at private RV resorts near towns for laundry and full hookups, 6 nights at state parks along the route, 2 nights at Harvest Hosts wineries, and 2 nights boondocking on BLM land outside a national park. At national-average rates, the private nights run about 4 × $58 ≈ $232, the state park nights run about 6 × $32 ≈ $192, and the Harvest Hosts and BLM nights are $0 in camping fees, though it's worth budgeting $20–30 per Harvest Hosts stop for the purchase that's the unwritten cost of admission. That totals roughly $424 in campground fees for 14 nights — an average of just over $30 a night — versus about $770 if all 14 nights had been booked at private parks. Shifting two more nights from private to public or free would push the total under $370.

howToSteps.title: Enter total nights
howToSteps.description: Count every night of the trip, from the first stop to the last, including any nights you haven't picked a campground for yet.

howToSteps.title: Break nights into private and public
howToSteps.description: Enter how many of those nights will be at private RV parks or resorts, and how many at public campgrounds — state parks, national parks, national forests, or Corps of Engineers lakes.

howToSteps.title: Add your free nights
howToSteps.description: Enter nights you expect to boondock, use Harvest Hosts, or stay somewhere with no camping fee — these add $0 to the total but still count toward total nights.

howToSteps.title: Calculate and compare to real rates
howToSteps.description: Click Calculate, then compare the average per night against actual listings for parks on your route — adjust the private/public split until the total matches what you're willing to spend.

tips: Passport America cuts the rate roughly in half at participating private parks (many land near $25–35/night instead of $50–70), but availability is often capped to one or two nights per stay and blacked out in peak season — check each park's restrictions before counting on the discount.

A Thousand Trails zone membership carries an annual fee (commonly $500–700 for one zone) but drops each night inside the system to $0 beyond that fee — it only pencils out if you're realistically racking up 25+ nights a year at parks that participate.

Harvest Hosts memberships (roughly $100/year) get you free overnight parking at wineries, farms, and breweries with zero hookups — budget $20–40 per stop for the purchase that's the unwritten cost of admission, and don't expect water or sewer.

Boondocking on BLM or national forest land is genuinely free, but factor in the generator fuel, extra battery capacity, or solar setup you'll lean on without shore power, plus the dump station and water fill you'll pay for every 4–7 days.

State and national park campgrounds book out 6 months ahead for summer weekends — if your trip depends on cheaper public sites, reserve the moment the window opens or your budget quietly shifts toward pricier private parks with same-day availability.
